fit: SNCA carrier phenotype and visual symptom history
assessment: SNCA duplication case histories, genetic results and a literature comparison describe motor and nonmotor presentations. Some duplication carriers had hallucinations, along with sleep and cognitive symptoms. The clinical feature is reported with genetic disease and does not measure a culinary effect.

fit: secondary Lewy body stimulation and imaging with overlapping study lineage
assessment: The secondary comparison selected 16 dementia with Lewy bodies participants and 19 controls with both imaging and stimulation measurements. Average early visual responses to checkerboards and resting perfusion were similar, while the relationship between stimulation threshold and visual response differed. The authors cite the earlier stimulation dataset. No oral fig comparison was made.

fit: visual review distinguishing function from experienced hallucinations
assessment: The clinical review examines Parkinson visual function from acuity and eye movements to perceptions and hallucinations. It discusses overlapping diagnoses and medication context. None of these narrative observations compares dried fig intake with a Parkinson hallucination endpoint.

fit: radiological differential and visual symptom phenotype
assessment: The completed AJNR review organizes causes of visual hallucinations by clinical presentation and characteristic imaging. Parkinson and Lewy body disease are part of a broader clinical differential. It summarizes imaging across conditions and does not present a fig study.

fit: past-month general neuropsychiatric inventory across dementia groups
assessment: A retrospective matched dementia comparison includes 125 Parkinson dementia, 250 dementia with Lewy bodies and 500 Alzheimer dementia cases. The past-month caregiver inventory uses a general hallucination item. Participant-level symptom comparisons across diagnoses do not supply a visual-only food effect.

fit: Parkinson drug withdrawal and case-level visual history
assessment: The clinical cohort follows dopamine agonist discontinuation and tabulates visual hallucinations in individual drug-related histories. The comparison concerns medication withdrawal. It does not identify dried fig intake or compare episode rates after meals.

fit: Parkinson visual phenotype and perception review
assessment: The review discusses distinct Parkinson visual measures, including acuity, visuoperceptual changes, illusions and formed visual hallucinations. Its clinical prevalence, genetic and pathophysiological summaries do not evaluate a dietary exposure.

fit: companion correspondence without an independent result cohort
assessment: This complete AJNR correspondence comments on the separate imaging review PMID26744445 and emphasizes molecular imaging in the visual hallucination differential. It supplies interpretive context without a new patient sample or fig comparison.

fit: postmortem histamine binding and prior visual symptom ratings
assessment: Postmortem receptor binding was compared with prior symptoms in Alzheimer and Lewy body dementia. The authors report a stronger psychotic-symptom association for delusions. The visual-specific group comparisons did not reach statistical significance. There is no dried fig exposure or episode rate.

fit: dementia clinical visual history and pulvinar visualization
assessment: The memory clinic series relates pulvinar visibility across MRI sequences to the presence of prior visual hallucinations in people with dementia. Time after a food exposure and Parkinson-specific episode counts were not measured.

fit: Parkinson GBA variant phenotype and time to first symptom
assessment: The Parkinson clinical and genetic study observes greater prevalence of visual hallucinations in mutation carriers than noncarriers (47% versus 22%) in the cited comparison. Time-to-event models estimate first progression to a feature. Neither measure isolates food intake or episode frequency.

fit: attention networks and neuropsychiatric group descriptors
assessment: The functional imaging comparison uses an attentional task in Lewy body dementia, Alzheimer dementia and controls. The hallucination subscale characterizes the groups. Task-linked network connectivity is the primary comparison, without a fig exposure.

fit: open-label Parkinson drug safety and people with visual adverse events
assessment: The open-label amantadine extension records visual hallucinations in 43 participants (19.3%). These are participants with a reported adverse event during follow-up, with no concurrent food comparison. Prior trial exposure and age are relevant to interpretation.

fit: psychological distress and a separate fluid-swallowing evidence family
assessment: The nonpharmacologic Lewy body dementia review includes psychological approaches addressing distress from visual hallucinations. The separate dietary fluid and postural trial addresses swallowing and aspiration. The distinct members provide no joint fig and visual outcome.

fit: postmortem pulvinar markers in dementia with Lewy bodies
assessment: The postmortem pulvinar comparison reports differences in transcripts and selected synaptic proteins in dementia with Lewy bodies. Clinical visual hallucinations frame the rationale. Tissue findings cannot supply the exposure or episode rate in the frozen claim.

fit: cause-specific patient proportions in very mild dementia
assessment: The retrospective very mild dementia series reports visual hallucinations in 31.6% of dementia with Lewy bodies, 11.4% of Parkinson dementia and 4.0% of Alzheimer dementia participants. These are proportions by diagnosis. Dried fig exposure and rates of episodes per patient were not measured.

fit: pooled clinical proportions with modality and ascertainment differences
assessment: The systematic review pools auditory and visual prevalence separately. Its visual prevalence estimate is 28.2% in Parkinson and 61.8% in dementia with Lewy bodies, with wide intervals and variation by ascertainment. The outcome is proportion of patients, with no exposure-stratified dried fig rate.

fit: Parkinson hallucination neuroimaging synthesis
assessment: The neuroimaging synthesis includes nine studies of Parkinson hallucination groups alongside separate dementia and cognitive analyses. Coordinate convergence and anatomical network projections address spatial localization. No underlying dried fig comparison or exposure-specific episode rate is reported.

fit: Parkinson binary visual history and substantia nigra sonography
assessment: Of 111 Parkinson patients with usable sonography, 18 reported visual hallucinations. The authors use presence as a binary outcome to model association with substantia nigra echogenicity and covariates. It is not an episode count or dietary comparison.

fit: experimental visual perception by established hallucination group
assessment: A laboratory visual learning task compares 17 Lewy body participants with hallucinations, 20 without and 20 controls. Prior visual templates improved disambiguation more in the hallucinator group. The task measures an effect of prior information on perception, without oral fig or clinical episode rates.

fit: walnut–fig syrup against active lactulose in older adults
assessment: The randomized 90-person functional constipation study reports responses in 43/45 on the combination versus 41/45 on lactulose (P=.677). Parkinson was exclusionary. It cannot isolate either ingredient. IRCT20200714048108N1 describes the same study with a two-week treatment scheme, while the paper describes four weeks.

fit: fig intervention against active fiber in a 20-person meeting abstract
assessment: At two weeks the fig arm improved in transit and defecation frequency from baseline. The authors report no clear arm difference across defecation symptoms. Earlier publication than the 40-person registry recruitment and a different cohort size and outcome window distinguish the records. The report has no Parkinson visual outcome.

fit: single-cohort caplet pilot combining flaxseed and fig extract
assessment: The 15 participants received flaxseed powder with extracted fig fruit and reported several bowel changes. The before–after pilot lacks a concurrent comparison and cannot isolate fig. The early DOI 10.17795/jjnpp-40069 and the later DOI identify one report family.

fit: canine fig paste phase and measured marker transit
assessment: Fifteen dogs passed through fixed successive periods. Fecal wet weight and transit improved during the fig-paste period relative to induced constipation. The sequential design leaves time and exposure inseparable. The diet and restriction remained during the paste period, and the right and rectosigmoid segment comparisons were unclear.

fit: fig paste in a drug-induced rat model of bowel dysfunction
assessment: The original abstract reports greater fecal output and intestinal transit length in fig paste groups. It addresses a different species, exposure form and outcome. Complete methods and numerical tables remain open.

fit: central Italian fieldwork on mixed dried fig decoction and other parts
assessment: The original tables place dried figs with other ingredients in a respiratory decoction and report separate latex and veterinary uses. The neighboring mallow entry is the one describing mild laxative use. Counts represent localities reporting customs. The fieldwork does not document changes in Parkinson visual episodes.

fit: ripe dried fruit extract, isolated rabbit gut and human platelets
assessment: The original abstract uses aqueous-ethanolic ripe dried fig fruit extract in isolated gut tissue and platelet assays. It reports preparation-level laboratory outcomes without an oral exposure, Parkinson group or visual symptom measure.
